examples.en: I wind the rope up from the well.
I slowly reeled in the fishing line.
If you roll up the blinds, the sunlight comes in.
I twisted my hair up and fixed it with a pin.
They wound up the anchor with a machine and the ship set off.
Be careful with your hands when you roll up the curtain.

explain: '감다'와 '올리다'가 합쳐진 말로, 줄이나 천을 돌려 감으면서 위로 올리는 동작이에요. 그냥 위로 올리면 '올리다', 줄을 당겨 올리면 '끌어올리다'를 쓰고, 감는 동작이 있을 때 '감아올리다'를 써요.
explain_en: It combines '감다' (to wind) and '올리다' (to raise), describing winding a rope or cloth while lifting it. If you just lift something, use '올리다', and if you pull it up, '끌어올리다'; use '감아올리다' when winding is involved.

examples.en: Involving even the family made the matter bigger.

examples.ko: 회사가 외부 전문가를 문제 해결에 개입시켰어요.
examples.en: The company brought an outside expert into solving the problem.
If you let emotions get into your work, your judgment gets cloudy.

examples.ko: 아이 싸움에 어른을 개입시킬 필요는 없어요.
examples.en: There's no need to get adults involved in a children's quarrel.

examples.ko: 저는 친구를 제 일에 개입시키고 싶지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't want to involve my friend in my business.

examples.ko: 사실만 말하고 의견은 개입시키지 않으려고 해요.
examples.en: I'll state only facts and try not to bring in my opinions.

explain: '개입하다'는 스스로 끼어드는 것이고, '개입시키다'는 다른 사람이나 감정을 끼어들게 하는 것이에요. '-을/를 -에 개입시키다'로 써요. '끼어들다'는 말 사이에 끼어들 때도 써서 더 일상적이에요.
explain_en: '개입하다' is stepping in yourself, but '개입시키다' is making another person or feeling get involved. The pattern is '-을/를 -에 개입시키다'. '끼어들다' is more everyday and also used for cutting into a conversation.

examples.ko: 이 도로는 군용 차량이 자주 다녀요.
examples.en: Military vehicles often travel on this road.

examples.ko: 군용 시설 근처에서는 사진을 찍으면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not take photos near military facilities.
A military plane passed through the sky.
Military blankets are thick and warm.
It was originally made for military use, so the watch is sturdy.

examples.ko: 이 땅은 군용지라서 들어갈 수 없어요.
examples.en: This land is military land, so you cannot go in.

explain: '군용 차', '군용 담요'처럼 다른 명사 앞에 붙여서 써요. 반대로 군대가 아닌 일반 사람이 쓰는 것은 '민간용'이라고 해요. 혼자 쓰이는 일은 드물어요.
explain_en: It goes in front of another noun, as in '군용 차' and '군용 담요'. For things used by ordinary people rather than the military, you say '민간용'. It rarely stands on its own.

examples.en: Please check the documents carefully.
He handles everything thoroughly.
I read the exam paper again carefully.
Look through the contract carefully and sign it.
When cleaning, I wiped even the corners carefully.

examples.ko: 메모를 꼼꼼히 남겨 두면 나중에 편해요.
examples.en: If you keep careful notes, it is easier later.

explain: '꼼꼼'은 '꼼꼼하다'의 어근이라 실제 대화에서는 '꼼꼼히', '꼼꼼하게', '꼼꼼한 사람'처럼 모양을 바꿔 써요. 반대로 대충 하는 것은 '대충'이나 '건성으로'라고 해요.
explain_en: 꼼꼼 is the root of 꼼꼼하다, so in real speech it appears as 꼼꼼히, 꼼꼼하게, or 꼼꼼한 사람. The opposite, doing something sloppily, is 대충 or '건성으로'.

examples.en: I failed the exam and was deeply discouraged.

examples.ko: 너무 낙담하지 말고 다시 해 봐요.
examples.en: Don't lose heart; let's try again.
I comforted my discouraged friend.

examples.ko: 그 소식을 듣고 낙담할 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.en: Hearing that news, I could not help but be disheartened.
He had a look of dismay on seeing the result.
People who don't lose heart even after failing are cool.

explain: 기대했던 일이 잘 안 되어서 힘이 빠질 때 써요. '실망하다'보다 마음이 더 무너지는 느낌이고, 말투가 조금 딱딱해요. 일상에서는 '속상하다', '힘이 빠지다'를 더 많이 말하고, 위로할 때는 '낙담하지 마세요'라고 해요.
explain_en: Used when something you hoped for fails and your energy drains. It feels like a heavier collapse of spirit than '실망하다' and sounds a bit stiff. In daily talk '속상하다' or '힘이 빠지다' are more common, and to comfort someone you say '낙담하지 마세요'.

examples.ko: 시험이 코앞에 닥쳐오니까 잠이 안 와요.
examples.en: The exam is right around the corner, so I can't sleep.

examples.ko: 태풍이 닥쳐온다는 뉴스를 보고 집에 일찍 갔어요.
examples.en: I saw the news that a typhoon was approaching and went home early.

examples.ko: 어려운 일이 닥쳐와도 포기하지 않을 거예요.
examples.en: I won't give up even when hard times come.

examples.ko: 이제 곧 마감이 닥쳐오는데 아직 반도 못 했어요.
examples.en: The deadline is almost here and I haven't even finished half.

examples.ko: 갑자기 닥쳐온 불행 앞에서 가족이 서로 힘이 되어 주었어요.
examples.en: Facing the misfortune that suddenly struck, the family supported each other.

examples.ko: 위기가 닥쳐왔지만 팀원들이 끝까지 힘을 냈어요.
examples.en: A crisis came, but the team members kept up their strength to the end.

explain: '다가오다'는 그냥 가까워지는 것이고, '닥쳐오다'는 시험, 위기, 태풍, 불행처럼 반갑지 않은 일이 바짝 가까워질 때 써요. 주어는 사람보다 일이나 상황인 경우가 많아요. '닥쳐오아'가 아니라 '닥쳐와요'로 줄여요.
explain_en: '다가오다' just means getting closer, while '닥쳐오다' is for unwelcome things like exams, crises, typhoons or misfortune closing in. The subject is usually an event or situation rather than a person. The polite form is '닥쳐와요', not '닥쳐오아요'.

examples.en: He denies the rumor.
The government denied responsibility.
You cannot deny the fact.
It looked strange that he denied it to the end.
He denied his mistake and got angry.
The company denied it, so the article was corrected.

explain: '아니라고 하다'와 비슷하지만 '부인하다'는 사실이나 혐의를 공식적으로 인정하지 않을 때 써요. 뉴스에서 자주 들려요. 같은 소리의 '부인(아내)'과 헷갈리지 않게 문장 속 쓰임을 보세요.
explain_en: Similar to saying 'it is not so', but this verb is for officially refusing to admit a fact or accusation, and it is common in the news. Do not confuse it with a same-sounding noun that means wife or married woman.

dis.h: deny an accusation or a fact

p.n: 부정하다 sounds like rejecting the truth itself, not just denying a charge.

examples.ko: 불이 나자 동네 사람들이 모여 불구경을 했어요.
examples.en: When a fire broke out, the neighbors gathered to watch it.
I heard that watching a fire used to be a big spectacle in the old days.
Everyone stopped to watch the fire, so the road was very congested.

examples.ko: 안전한 곳에서 불구경하지 말고 신고부터 하세요.
examples.en: Do not just watch the fire from a safe place; report it first.

examples.ko: 남의 일을 불구경하듯 보면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You should not look at other people's problems like a bystander.

examples.ko: 불구경 나온 사람들 때문에 소방차가 지나가기 어려웠어요.
examples.en: The fire truck had trouble getting through because of the people who came out to watch.

explain: 실제로 불이 난 곳을 구경하는 일이지만, '불구경하듯'처럼 남의 일을 가만히 보기만 하는 태도를 말할 때도 써요. 실제 화재에서는 구경보다 신고와 대피가 먼저예요.

phrases.example: 회사가 어려운데 다들 강 건너 불구경하듯 해요.
phrases.en: The company is in trouble, but everyone acts as if it has nothing to do with them.
phrases.nuance_ko: 자기와 상관없는 일이라며 걱정 없이 지켜보기만 하는 태도를 말해요. 비판하거나 서운할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: It describes watching passively, as if a problem has nothing to do with you. People use it when criticizing or feeling hurt by such an attitude.

explain_en: It literally means watching a fire, but '불구경하듯' is also used for watching someone else's problem passively. In a real fire, reporting it and evacuating come before watching.

examples.en: I went on a mountain hike with friends on the weekend.
It rained during the hike, so we came down.
This hike takes about three hours.
Gloves are a must for winter hikes.
I checked the hiking course in advance.
My father goes to a hiking club every month.

explain: '등산'과 거의 같지만 '산행'은 산길을 걷는 일정 전체의 느낌이 있어서 '산행 코스', '산행 모임'처럼 써요. 일상에서는 '등산'이 더 흔하고, 산악회 안내문이나 후기에서 '산행'이 자주 보여요.
explain_en: Nearly the same as '등산', but '산행' feels like the whole trek along mountain paths, so you get '산행 코스' and '산행 모임'. '등산' is more common in daily talk; '산행' shows up in hiking-club notices and trip reports.

examples.en: I hope everyone stays healthy.
He always wished for his family to be happy.
I wrote a piece wishing for peace in the new year.
The thing I had hoped for finally came true.
We said goodbye wishing each other success.
If you wish earnestly, a way will open.

explain: '바라다'와 뜻은 가깝지만 '소망하다'는 더 간절하고 진지한 느낌이라 인사말, 편지, 기도, 글에서 자주 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '바라요', '빌어요'가 더 자연스러워요. 같은 뜻의 명사는 '소망'이고 '소원'과 거의 비슷하게 써요.
explain_en: Close to '바라다' (to hope), but 소망하다 feels more earnest and serious, so it appears in greetings, letters, prayers, and writing. In daily talk, '바라요' or '빌어요' sound more natural. The noun '소망' is used almost like '소원' (a wish).

examples.en: The court judged this case fairly.
Citizens judge politicians through elections.
It is hard for one person to judge another.

examples.ko: 신이 모든 사람을 심판한다고 믿는 사람도 있어요.
examples.en: Some people believe God judges everyone.
They asked for the wrongdoer to be judged.

examples.ko: 먼저 사정을 듣고 나서 심판해야 해요.
examples.en: You have to hear the circumstances first and then judge.

explain: 경기에서 심판을 볼 때는 '심판을 보다'라고 해요. '심판하다'는 잘잘못을 가려 판정을 내린다는 무거운 느낌이라 재판이나 선거 이야기에 어울려요. '판단하다', '평가하다'보다 훨씬 강하게 들려요.
explain_en: For refereeing a game, say '심판을 보다'. '심판하다' feels heavy, like weighing right and wrong and passing judgment, so it fits talk about trials and elections. It sounds much stronger than '판단하다' or '평가하다'.

examples.en: I didn't mean to say that.
Let's think about what the author intended.
I didn't do it on purpose.
It didn't go the way I intended.

examples.ko: 광고를 만든 사람은 사람들이 웃도록 의도했어요.
examples.en: The person who made the ad intended people to laugh.

examples.ko: 그 일을 처음부터 의도했다면 더 큰 문제가 돼요.
examples.en: If you intended that from the start, it becomes a bigger problem.

explain: '의도'는 마음속의 목적이에요. 사과할 때 '의도하지 않았어요'라고 말할 수 있어요. '일부러'는 더 일상적인 말이에요.
explain_en: '의도' is the purpose in your mind. When apologizing you can say '의도하지 않았어요'. '일부러' is the more casual everyday word.

examples.en: The soldiers kept advancing forward.
The car parked by repeatedly moving forward and backward.
Even a small step forward matters.

examples.ko: 팀은 결승 진출로 한 걸음 전진했어요.
examples.en: The team took a step forward by reaching the final.
The robot moves when you press the forward button.
The teacher told us not to stop moving forward.

explain: 전진은 앞으로 나아가는 것이에요. 반대말은 '후진'이고, 자동차 기어에서도 '전진'과 '후진'으로 나눠요. 일이 앞으로 발전할 때도 비유로 쓸 수 있어요.
explain_en: 전진 is moving forward. The opposite is '후진', and car gears are also split into 전진 and 후진. It can also be used figuratively for making progress.

examples.en: A new problem was raised.
Various opinions are raised in the meeting.
I'll answer the questions being raised one by one.
When a problem is raised, we check right away.
Let's solve the problems already raised first.
I explained every time a doubt was raised.

explain: 문제, 의혹, 질문 같은 말이 나올 때만 써요. 앞에 보통 '문제가', '의견이'가 와요. 사람이 꺼내면 '제기하다'예요.
explain_en: Use it only when issues, doubts, or questions come up. It is usually preceded by '문제가' or '의견이'. When a person raises it, use '제기하다'.

examples.en: The director cast a new actor.

examples.ko: 제작사는 유명한 가수를 캐스팅하고 싶어 해요.
examples.en: The production company wants to cast a famous singer.

examples.ko: 그 역할에 누구를 캐스팅할지 고민 중이에요.
examples.en: We are thinking about who to cast in that role.
I watched a video of the casting process.
A news story said they had cast the lead.

examples.ko: 어린이 역은 오디션 없이 캐스팅하기로 했어요.
examples.en: We decided to cast the children's roles without an audition.

explain: '배우를 캐스팅하다'처럼 고르는 쪽이 주어예요. 뽑힌 배우 쪽에서는 '캐스팅되다'를 써요. 길에서 배우나 모델 후보를 찾는 것은 '길거리 캐스팅'이라고 해요.
explain_en: The one choosing is the subject, as in '배우를 캐스팅하다' (cast an actor). From the chosen actor's side, '캐스팅되다' is used. Finding acting or modeling talent on the street is called '길거리 캐스팅' (street casting).

examples.en: I stacked the bowls one by one and put them in the cupboard.

examples.ko: 의자를 포개 놓으면 자리를 덜 차지해요.
examples.en: If you stack the chairs, they take up less space.

examples.ko: 아이가 손을 내 손 위에 포갰어요.
examples.en: The child laid her hand on top of mine.
If you stack paper cups too high, they fall over.
If you stack the T-shirts, the closet looks neat.

examples.ko: 두 사람이 다리를 포개고 앉아 있어요.
examples.en: The two of them are sitting with their legs crossed one over the other.

explain: 같은 모양의 물건을 위에 겹쳐서 놓을 때 써요. 그릇, 의자, 손처럼 서로 맞게 겹치는 느낌이 있어요. 높이 쌓을 때는 '쌓다'를 더 많이 쓰고, 종이를 접어 겹칠 때는 '겹치다'가 자연스러워요.
explain_en: Use it for laying items of the same shape on top of one another, like bowls, chairs or hands, so they fit together. For tall piles, '쌓다' is more common, and for overlapping paper, '겹치다' sounds natural.
